analysis.one_liner: Permanently exempts overseas banking, financing, and insurance profits of US multinationals from a US anti-deferral tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: US tax law generally taxes American shareholders of foreign subsidiaries they control on certain kinds of passive or easily-shifted income. This bill would permanently carve out profits earned by overseas arms of banks, finance companies, and insurance businesses from those rules, so those 'active financing' profits would not be taxed to the US shareholder until — and unless — paid out as dividends. That lets large financial companies defer, and often avoid, US tax on income booked abroad. The bill was introduced in March 2005 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational banks, finance companies, and insurance companies with controlled foreign corporations would gain a permanent exemption from subpart F, allowing them to defer or avoid US tax on active financing income earned overseas. Shareholders of those firms benefit indirectly. The federal Treasury would bear the forgone revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Amends section 954(h) by striking paragraph (9), removing the scheduled expiration of the special rule that excludes income of banking, financing, or similar businesses from subpart F foreign personal holding company income.
Amends section 953(e) by striking paragraph (10), similarly removing the expiration of the exemption for insurance income earned in the active conduct of an insurance business.

Per the CRS summary, the bill permanently extends the subpart F exemption for active financing income — insurance, banking, financing, or similar businesses — earned on overseas operations of controlled foreign corporations.
The change applies to taxable years of foreign corporations beginning after enactment, making the exemption permanent rather than temporary.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the US Treasury — and ultimately general taxpayers — would bear the cost of revenue forgone, since profits shifted to foreign financing and insurance subsidiaries would no longer be subject to current US tax at the shareholder level. Ordinary taxpayers gain nothing directly from the bill; its benefits flow to the financial companies and their shareholders.

drawbacks.text: The bill's only beneficiaries are financial businesses with foreign operations; it contains no provision benefiting individual or ordinary taxpayers, so its cost falls on the general revenue base that funds government for everyone.

Permanent expensing of a deferral advantage for active financing income would entrench a channel through which financial groups can book income in low-tax jurisdictions and delay or avoid US tax on it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are concentrated and one-sided: a permanent tax deferral advantage for multinational banks, finance companies, and insurers, with the cost showing up as reduced federal revenue borne by everyone else. There is no offsetting public benefit in the bill text; the honest case for it rests on industry arguments about competitiveness of US financial firms abroad, which the bill's materials themselves do not document.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced in March 2005, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2005 by Rep. Jim McCrery with 16 original cosponsors and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
That referral was the bill's only action; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action for the remainder of the Congress.
It collected 30 cosponsors — 24 Republicans and 6 Democrats — before the Congress ended without the bill ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, multinational financial firms did not obtain a permanent exemption from subpart F taxation of their overseas financing and insurance income, and the federal revenue base was spared that permanent cost. No one gained an affirmative benefit from the outcome beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the exemption never became law

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, markup, or committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan on paper — 24 of 30 cosponsors were Republicans but 6 were Democrats, including Ways and Means members like Richard Neal and Jim McDermott — while the bill's death came from committee inaction, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would permanently exempt their overseas banking and financing profits from subpart F anti-deferral rules, letting them defer or avoid US tax on income booked through foreign subsidiaries. The benefit flows to the firms and their shareholders; the cost is forgone federal revenue borne by general taxpayers.

Striking paragraph (10) of section 953(e) would permanently exempt insurance income earned abroad from current US taxation of the US shareholder, a permanent revenue cost to the Treasury with no direct benefit to policyholders or the public.
